blocks.prompt: A Bike With an Engine
blocks.text: A motorcycle is like a bicycle with an engine. It has two wheels, a seat, and handlebars. The rider twists the right handle to go faster. This is called the throttle. To slow down, the rider squeezes the brakes. A motorcycle can go many miles on a little bit of gas. That makes it cheap to ride. Riders wear a helmet, gloves, and a thick jacket. If they fall, the gear keeps them safe. When the motorcycle leans into a turn, it can go around a corner without tipping over. Fast wheels help it stay balanced and upright.

blocks.prompt: The Machine That Balances Itself
blocks.text: A motorcycle looks simple, but keeping it upright is a clever trick. When you push a bicycle without a rider, it can roll a long way on its own before it tips. The same is true for a motorcycle. As the wheels spin, they resist falling over, and the way the front wheel is built lets the bike steer itself back under its weight. This is why a moving motorcycle feels steady while a stopped one wants to fall. Riders steer in a surprising way. To turn left at speed, a rider gently pushes the left handle forward. The bike leans left, and around the corner it goes. This is called countersteering, and every rider does it, even if they do not notice. The first motorcycle was built in Germany in 1885 by Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach. It had a wooden frame and a small gas engine. It was slow and shaky, but it proved that an engine could move two wheels down a road. Today motorcycles carry people all over the world.

blocks.prompt: The Physics Hiding in Two Wheels
blocks.text: To a person standing on the curb, a motorcycle is a mystery. It has only two wheels, yet a rider can cruise for miles without tipping over. The secret is motion. A spinning wheel behaves like a spinning top. It resists any push that would tilt it, an effect called gyroscopic stability. Just as important is the shape of the front fork, which is angled so that the front wheel naturally rolls back underneath the bike whenever it starts to lean. Together these forces make a moving motorcycle want to stay upright. Steering a motorcycle is stranger than steering a car. At any real speed, a rider turns by countersteering: a light push on the left grip to go left, a light push on the right grip to go right. The push makes the bike lean, and the lean carries it through the curve. Riders learn this by feel long before anyone explains the physics to them. Under the seat sits the engine, measured in cubic centimeters, or cc. A larger number usually means more power. The engine sends its power through a chain to the back wheel, and the rider changes gears with a lever worked by the left foot. A skilled rider blends throttle, brakes, clutch, and balance without thinking. Motorcycles matter for more than fun. They use far less fuel than cars, fit through crowded traffic, and reach villages where wide roads never went. In many countries they are the main way families and goods move from place to place.

blocks.prompt: Ordinary Physics, Working Faster Than the Eye
blocks.text: Balancing a motorcycle looks like magic, but it is ordinary physics working faster than the eye. Two effects do most of the work. The first is gyroscopic stability: a spinning wheel stores energy in its motion and resists being tilted, the same reason a spinning top does not fall. The second, and the more powerful, is the geometry of the front end. The steering axis meets the ground slightly ahead of where the tire touches down, a distance engineers call trail. Trail makes the front wheel behave like the caster on a shopping cart, swinging around to point straight and steering itself back beneath the bike the instant it begins to lean. A parked motorcycle falls over. A rolling one fights to stand up. Because of this, riders steer in a way that feels backward until it becomes instinct. To begin a left turn at speed, a rider pushes gently on the left grip, which momentarily steers the front wheel right. The bike drops into a left lean, and the same self-correcting geometry then carries it smoothly around the curve. This is countersteering, and every experienced rider does it without conscious thought. The machine itself is a chain of simple parts working together. The engine, sized in cubic centimeters, burns fuel to spin a crankshaft. That power flows through a clutch and gearbox and down a chain to the rear wheel. The rider controls speed with a twist grip throttle, changes gears with the left foot, and manages two separate brakes for the front and rear wheels. Coordinating all of this while balancing is a real skill, which is why riders train before they take to busy roads. Motorcycles were born in 1885, when Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach bolted a small gas engine to a wooden two wheeler in Germany. Within a few decades the design had spread worldwide. Today motorcycles are far more than a hobby. They sip fuel, slip through jammed city streets, and carry people and cargo along narrow tracks that cars cannot manage. In much of Asia, Africa, and South America, the motorcycle, not the car, is the vehicle that keeps daily life moving.

blocks.prompt: Forever Upright: The Two Tricks Inside a Motorcycle
blocks.text: Ask most people how a motorcycle stays upright and they will point to the rider, as if balance were pure human skill. The truth is more interesting. A motorcycle is largely self-balancing, and a good rider spends less effort holding it up than gently guiding forces that are already at work. Understanding those forces turns a mysterious machine into an elegant one. Two effects share the job of keeping a moving bike vertical. The first is gyroscopic stability. A spinning wheel is a store of angular momentum, and angular momentum resists change in direction. Try to tilt a spinning wheel and it pushes back, which is why a rolling wheel stands while a still one topples. The second effect, and the one engineers consider more important, is a piece of geometry called trail. The front wheel's steering axis, if extended to the ground, strikes the pavement slightly in front of the tire's contact point. That small distance makes the front wheel act like a furniture caster: whenever the bike leans, the wheel automatically swivels in the direction of the lean and steers the machine back underneath its own weight. A modern motorcycle is engineered so that these forces cooperate. The result is a vehicle that, once rolling, genuinely wants to stay up. This physics explains one of the strangest facts about riding: at speed, you steer a motorcycle by turning the handlebars the wrong way. To carve a left curve, a rider presses forward on the left grip. For a fraction of a second the front wheel points right, which tips the whole machine into a left lean, and trail then guides it gracefully around the corner. The technique is called countersteering, and although every fast rider relies on it, most learned it by feel and are surprised to hear it described. The machine that harnesses all this is a tidy sequence of parts. An engine, measured in cubic centimeters, burns fuel to turn a crankshaft. The power passes through a clutch and a gearbox, then runs down a chain or belt to the rear wheel. The rider meters power with a twist of the right grip, selects gears with the left foot, and works independent front and rear brakes. Doing all of that while reading traffic is why riding is a trained skill rather than a casual one. None of this is old. The first true motorcycle appeared in 1885, when the German engineers Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach fixed a small gasoline engine to a wooden frame with two main wheels. Their machine was slow and rough, yet it settled a question that mattered: an engine could drive two wheels down a road and stay balanced. From that shaky prototype grew a global industry. Today the motorcycle is not mainly a toy. It burns little fuel, threads through gridlocked cities, and reaches roads too narrow or too rough for cars. Across much of Asia, Africa, and Latin America, it is the everyday vehicle that carries workers, students, and goods, the quiet engine of ordinary life.
